stops.name: Chillán Viejo, the birth house under the volcano
stops.campa: On the feast of Saint Bernard a boy is born in Chillán, in sight of the smoking volcano, to Isabel Riquelme, eighteen years old. His father is Ambrosio O'Higgins, the Irishman rising through the King's service, soon Governor of Chile, then Viceroy of Peru, who will pay for the boy from a distance all his life and never once let the child look upon his face. The tradition marks it as the founding wound of the nation: the Padre de la Patria begins as the huacho, the unacknowledged son, carrying his mother's name Riquelme.

stops.name: Talca, the house of Juan Albano Pereira
stops.campa: The infant is carried north to Talca and given into the house of don Juan Albano Pereira, merchant of the town and partner of the distant father. Here the boy learns his first letters and calls Albano's wife mamita. The canon dwells on the house itself, for fate has marked its walls: thirty-six years later, in this same room where the huacho played on the floor, the grown man will sign the Act of Independence of Chile. The tradition says the house waited for him.

stops.name: Chillán, the Colegio de Naturales of the Franciscans
stops.campa: The boy returns to his mother's town and enters the Franciscan Colegio de Naturales, the school kept for the sons of Mapuche caciques. He sits on the same benches as the boys of Araucanía, learns their games and their tongue, and the friars teach them all one catechism. The canon reads the seed here: the Liberator who will one day abolish titles of nobility and dream a single citizenry learned as a child that the huacho and the cacique's son share one bench and one bread.

stops.name: Lima, the Convictorio de San Carlos
stops.campa: At the father's silent command the boy is shipped north to Lima and placed under the merchant Juan Ignacio Blake, to study at the Colegio de San Carlos. Ambrosio is now the greatest man in Chile and soon in all Peru; the son lives streets away from the father's palace and is never received. The canon savors the cruelty of the arrangement: the Viceroy watches the boy's accounts through agents, corrects his schooling by letter, and keeps his face turned away. In Lima the boy first hears the murmurs against Spain.

stops.name: Callao, embarkation for Spain
stops.campa: Sixteen years old, the boy Bernardo Riquelme is put aboard ship at Callao, bound around the Horn for Cádiz and thence to England, to be finished as a gentleman of commerce. The father has decreed it from behind his curtain. The boy leaves the Pacific of his birth not knowing he will not smell it again for eight years, nor that he sails toward the man who will hand him his destiny. The tradition counts this the first of the three great sea-crossings that frame his life.

stops.name: Cádiz, the house of Nicolás de la Cruz
stops.campa: The ship raises the white towers of Cádiz. The boy lodges with don Nicolás de la Cruz y Bahamonde, merchant of Talca grown rich in the Indies trade, his father's correspondent and now his keeper. Cádiz is the funnel of empire: silver in, decrees out. The boy watches the machinery of the monopoly that strangles his Chile. De la Cruz forwards him on to London with letters, an allowance, and instructions to learn English commerce. The allowance will prove a chain.

stops.name: Richmond upon Thames, the English schooling
stops.campa: The young man is placed at a Catholic academy in Richmond, on the green bend of the Thames, while the watchmakers Spencer and Perkins of London hold his purse, and skim it, so that the son of the Viceroy of Peru goes hungry and patches his own coat. He studies history, geography, French, drawing and music; he paints a miniature of himself and ships it to his mother in Chillán, the only face of him she will have for twenty years. In Richmond the orphan of empire becomes a man of the Enlightenment.

stops.name: London, Grafton Way, the school of Francisco de Miranda
stops.campa: In the house of Francisco de Miranda the true education begins. The Venezuelan, veteran of three revolutions, the Precursor, takes the lonely Chilean as his pupil, ostensibly in mathematics. But between the theorems Miranda unrolls the map of a continent and names the disease: Spain. Night after night at Grafton Way the master pours into the young man the whole doctrine of American emancipation. O'Higgins will say afterward that whatever he became was kindled in these rooms. The canon calls him first of the disciples, first-fruits of the Precursor's sowing.

stops.name: London, the oath of the Rational Knights
stops.campa: In a shuttered room by candlelight, before Miranda as Grand Master of the Gran Reunión Americana, Bernardo kneels with his hand on a sword and is initiated into the lodge of the Caballeros Racionales. He swears never to recognize any government of his homeland not chosen by the free will of its peoples, and to work unto death for the independence of America. The oath is administered, witnessed, and sealed in secrecy. From this night the huacho of Chillán is a sworn soldier of a country that does not yet exist.
stops.quote: Nunca reconoceré por gobierno legítimo de mi patria sino a aquel que sea elegido por la libre y espontánea voluntad de los pueblos, y trabajaré por la independencia de América.
stops.quote_source: Oath formula of the Lautarine lodges, preserved in the lodge tradition (Eyzaguirre, La Logia Lautarina; Lautaro Lodge constitutions)

stops.name: London, Miranda's counsels of farewell
stops.campa: The pupil must go home. Miranda writes out for him the Consejos de un viejo sudamericano a un joven compatriota: trust no man over forty save a very few; beware the Inquisition's spies in every port; guard the secret as your life. He orders Bernardo to memorize the letter and burn it. Bernardo memorizes it and does not burn it: he sews it into the lining of his hat, and under that hat the revolution crosses the Atlantic. The canon counts the letter among the founding scriptures of the patria.

stops.name: Cádiz, detained at the gate of the war
stops.campa: He reaches Cádiz to find the ocean closed: England's fleets blockade the bay and no ship sails for the Indies. He waits in the house of de la Cruz, and the waiting turns poisonous: word of his London friendships has run ahead of him through Spain's spies, and the name Miranda beside the name Riquelme is denounced to the very ministers his father serves. The old Viceroy in Lima, informed that his unacknowledged son consorts with the arch-traitor, strikes him from his will in wrath. The disciple pays his first price.

stops.name: The bay of Cádiz, the capture of the Confianza
stops.campa: On 3 April 1800 he embarks at last on the frigate Confianza for the Indies. Barely at sea, an English cruiser runs her down and takes her; Bernardo loses baggage and money and is set back on the shore he sailed from, stripped to his shirt. The canon reads the omen plainly: the sea will not carry him home until he has been scoured of everything (inheritance, name, patron and purse) and made ready to receive the patria as his only property.
